harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First pods come roughly two months after sowing, this crop's own days to maturity, and the vine keeps bearing progressively after that.

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: The vines bear for about nine to ten weeks before slowing and are pulled as they decline. Pod set likely slows through the hottest stretch of the Mojave summer, but the chart shades pole beans through a single unbroken spring-into-summer block rather than the two-window gap it gives bush beans, so no separate heat exclusion is modeled here.

basil.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start seed indoors in early February, about six weeks ahead of the mid-March set-out, so transplants are ready once frost risk passes; kept to early February so January stays a dormant month here.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Set basil transplants out in mid-March once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, per UNR Extension's warm-season vegetable window of March through May (FS-02-61).

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: First cuttings come about 75 days after transplant.

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Basil is frost-tender and keeps producing until the first fall frost; give it afternoon shade once daytime highs push past 100°F in peak summer, but do not stop harvesting.

basil.region_notes_beginner: In the Las Vegas Valley, start basil seed indoors in early February and set transplants out in mid-March once frost is past. It keeps growing right through the desert summer with no pause, but the sun is intense here, so once daytime highs climb past about 100°F give it afternoon shade or light shade cloth and water at the base rather than on the leaves. Harvest continues into fall until the first frost, typically late November.
basil.region_notes_seasoned: University of Nevada, Reno Extension places basil in the warm-season window that runs March through May (FS-02-61). Basil does not pause for the Mojave summer the way cool-season crops do, but once highs push past 100°F give it afternoon shade or 30 to 40 percent shade cloth and water deeply at the root zone; the dry air here keeps foliar disease pressure low. Harvest runs continuously into fall until frost, around late November in zone 9, a couple weeks earlier at the cooler zone 8 edge and later at Laughlin.
